quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: Section 21 satisfies the preferred position on its material terms and comfortably clears the fallback. The cap in 21.1 is expressly mutual ("The cap is mutual"), set at the greater of Fees paid or payable in the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000; "Fees" (1.5) means recurring subscription, professional services and usage fees payable under an Order Form, so the basis is meaningful rather than illusory. Section 21.2 excludes indirect and consequential damages mutually ("neither Party is liable"), and helpfully confirms restoration of Customer Data, replacement services, notices and incident response are direct damages. Section 21.3 places outside the cap each Party's breach of confidentiality, data-protection or security obligations, indemnification obligations, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud, and infringement or misappropriation of the other Party's IP — covering every carve-out we require. Two points are noted rather than redlined: the payment carve-out is limited to "undisputed Fees for conforming Services" rather than all Customer amounts due (taxes, expenses and interest are outside the "Fees" definition), and 21.2's exclusion is qualified "to the extent those damages are legally excludable"; neither is material given 21.4 (savings language, independent caps surviving failure of an exclusive remedy) and 18.2 (insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities). No hidden or one-sided cap appears in the warranty (19.4) or indemnity (Section 20) provisions.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.

verification.notes: All eight preferred elements are met in operative language: § 22.1 as rendered supplies frequency (once per 12 months), 30 days' written notice, business hours, off-site where possible, and an independent auditor bound by confidentiality; § 22.2 already supplies the 5% cost-shift threshold and the express no-direct-access bar, and both were retained verbatim. The walk-away features of the original § 22.1 (unlimited, unannounced audits and remote system access) are removed, and the contradiction with § 22.2's no-direct-access sentence is resolved rather than left dangling. Minimality holds: the edit replaces only the single offending sentence in § 22.1, which had to be rewritten in full because every one of its terms (timing, notice, remote access) was non-compliant; no survival tails, procedures, expense allocations, or other extras were added, and the Customer-favourable § 22.2 carve-outs (Customer Data unrelated to usage, privileged material, another supplier's confidential information) were left untouched. Intent is preserved: Vendor retains a usage-verification right, the cost-shift and shortfall-payment mechanic in § 22.2 continues to operate against the audit right in § 22.1, and no cross-reference or defined term is left undefined. Fallback level is not independently complete only because the retained cost trigger sits at five percent rather than ten percent; no repair is required since the position is complete at the preferred level.

Our position is no non-solicitation restriction on the customer; if you need one, we can accept a mutual 12-month covenant limited to personnel directly involved in the Services, with general-advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs and no prohibition on hiring.

quote: 12.4 For eighteen months after termination Customer will not solicit or engage any person employed by Vendor at any time during the term.
rationale: Section 12.4 is the only non-solicitation provision in the document and it fails every material fallback element: it is one-way against Customer only, runs eighteen months (and from termination rather than from the end of a person's involvement), covers any person employed by Vendor at any time during the term rather than only personnel directly involved in the Services, bars "engage" and so operates as a no-hire, and has no general-advertising or unsolicited-approach carve-out. It also contradicts § 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no no-hire commitment. Because the fallback would require rewriting the entire one-sentence covenant, we take the preferred position and remove the restriction on Customer, offering the narrow mutual 12-month fallback in the comment.

elements.element: Customer has no non-solicitation restriction.

elements.element: The restriction lasts no longer than 12 months after the person's involvement ends.
elements.evidence: Vacuously satisfied — the eighteen-month post-termination period is removed entirely; no duration operates because no covenant remains.

elements.element: General advertisements are excluded from the restriction.
elements.evidence: No restriction remains to which a carve-out could attach; § 12.3 separately preserves Customer's freedom to hire "any person who responds to general recruitment."

verification.notes: Preferred checklist is complete: the sole non-solicit binding Customer (§ 12.4) is replaced with an unconditional statement that Customer is subject to no non-solicitation restriction, leaving no residual solicit/engage/no-hire mechanic. Fallback elements are vacuously satisfied because the removal of the covenant eliminates the condition each element constrains; no mutual covenant was added, which is correct for the preferred target. Minimal: the edit is confined to the offending sentence in § 12.4. Favourable § 12.3 is retained verbatim, no survival tail, procedure, or extra obligation is added, and no words outside the target element are deleted. Replacing the sentence with a short declaratory clause rather than deleting the subsection avoids a numbering gap and adds no new requirement. Preserves intent: no cross-references point to § 12.4, no defined term is orphaned, and the retained § 12.3 acknowledgement (no no-hire commitment) is now consistent rather than contradicted by § 12.4. Classification as a deviation is correct — the original clause failed the fallback on every material term (one-way, 18 months from termination, all Vendor employees at any time, "engage" no-hire, no carve-outs), and the walk-away triggers (no-hire, all-personnel scope) were present.

rationale: Order Forms auto-renew for twelve months, but the non-renewal notice window is 180 days — beyond the fallback maximum of 60 days and within walk-away territory (windows longer than 90 days). The pricing limb already beats our position: § 8.3 caps renewal increases at the lesser of CPI and three percent. We therefore target the fallback level and make the single smallest change, shortening the window to sixty (60) days (numeral included for clarity); the renewal term is already twelve months and no Vendor reminder mechanic exists (a preferred-only sub-element noted but not flagged).

elements.element: If renewal is automatic, Customer's non-renewal notice window is no more than 60 days.
elements.evidence: Rendered § 8.2 shortens the window from one hundred eighty days to "sixty (60) days' advance written notice", which is at (not above) the 60-day fallback maximum; the deterministic check "non-renewal notice window ≤ 60 days" also passed.

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: the single edit brings the non-renewal notice window to exactly 60 days, and the pre-existing § 8.3 CPI/3% cap already sits inside the 5% fallback ceiling. Preferred level is not reached: the opt-out remains 60 days rather than 30, and no 60-day pre-renewal Vendor reminder obligation exists. Targeting the fallback is a legitimate choice, but the drafter should note these as preferred-only gaps (as the rationale does) rather than claim preferred coverage. The original 180-day window exceeded the 90-day walk-away threshold, so classifying the clause as a deviation and redlining it is correct; the 12-month renewal term was already compliant and was properly left untouched. Minimality holds: only the numeral in § 8.2 changed (one hundred eighty days → sixty (60) days). § 8.3's uplift cap, 90-day increase notice, and prepaid-period protection — all Customer-favourable — were retained verbatim, and no survival tails, procedures, or extraneous requirements were added. The added parenthetical numeral sits inside the words being replaced and is not a separate cosmetic edit. Intent is preserved: the mutual "either Party" structure, the Order Form-level renewal mechanic, the twelve-month renewal term, and all pricing timing mechanics survive without contradiction; no defined term or cross-reference is left dangling.

quote: 11.1 Upon expiry or termination for any reason, Vendor shall, at Customer's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for up to six months at the rates in the expiring Order Form. Assistance includes knowledge transfer, export support, cooperation with a replacement supplier, orderly migration, and continued service at the then-current scope and service levels.
rationale: Section 11 satisfies the preferred position on its material terms. § 11.1 applies "Upon expiry or termination for any reason" and gives up to six months of transition assistance (knowledge transfer, export support, migration, cooperation with a replacement supplier, continued service at the same scope and service levels). Pricing is fixed at "the rates in the expiring Order Form", which is at least as favourable to us as the preferred "then-current rates" because it removes exposure to a price uplift, so it is not a deviation. § 11.2 requires return of all Customer Data within thirty days in a "complete, commonly used, documented, machine-readable format" with relationships and metadata, and expressly bars withholding data over a fee dispute; the thirty-day clock runs from our own request, a trigger we control, so post-termination return is assured. § 11.3 requires secure deletion from active systems and backups after we confirm successful return, with written certification by an authorized officer, and confines any law-required retained copy to protected, non-use status — i.e. certified deletion occurs after return, as preferred. § 16.5 confirms Customer Data remains governed by Sections 11 and 15, so no other clause cuts across this. No walk-away features (no immediate deletion, no denial of return) appear anywhere in the document.
